examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/2b22742201ba6932de40a628419faef0405bc8ae0ad26814bc7ca515455e3e5c.png)
Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute $\Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t)$ and the particular solution $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ of the system.
examples.worked_solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

In our case,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071383/assets/0c7accec33fc7c9d6b2a228c8ec4bcc454f687be7f96ab615b3b818f82fb8cc8.png)

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-2{e}^{-4t})-2{e}^{-4t}\cdot {e}^{3t}}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{3t} & -2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{t} \\ -\frac{17}{10}{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{17}{10}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
